# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two

**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 74, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
training modalities**, typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
concentration; (3) the typical frequency of workouts in high-performance training (6-12 a
week) dictates certain conditions for the session after a key-workout: it should show a
significant load reduction, and running two consecutive key-workouts, while possible, risks
excessive load concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be
"substantially reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of
muscle restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance sport; the
daily program for juniors, for example, may be more diverse, multilateral, and therefore
more attractive. Figure 2.4 maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary
additions to five dominant ones: aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint,
strength-endurance-aerobic, and hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic
endurance pairs with strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed
aerobic-anaerobic endurance; alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive
strength, hypertrophy-strength (after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs
with neural-strength, flexibility, and aerobic restoration; and, when learning new technical
elements is the dominant task, any kind of training modality may be added, but only *after*
the dominant, technical-learning task, not before it. Table 2.12 gives the
physiological/psychological rationale for
several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).

**Why it works: the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours); these read as
the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
citations to a dose-response study.

**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline:** the class-1 lecture (transcript pp.28-29)
presents this same Figure 2.4 chart, and the course attributes its block-periodization
material to Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.64); "incompatible qualities... are not both
targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29, "you can't ride two
horses with one saddle") is the same instinct at the block level rather than the
single-session level. This Issurin entry gives that instinct a specific numeric structure
(≤3 modalities, 65-70% time-share) that the baseline material does not itself repeat at the
session level.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the ≤3-modality, 65-70%, and 20-hour figures as
Issurin's own heuristics rather than established constants: no citation or underlying data
is given for any of the three in this chapter. Issurin explicitly narrows the number
constraints to high-performance training; junior/developmental programming is stated to
reasonably need more variety, not fewer modalities. Figure 2.4's compatibility map is not
exhaustive (it covers five dominant modalities, not every possible combination); an
untested pairing should not be assumed incompatible or compatible by default; Issurin gives
no guidance for modalities not shown in the figure.

**Example** — **Inference:** a practice plan combining strength-endurance, aerobic-anaerobic
conditioning, maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would
have four distinct modalities, exceeding the stated ≤3 rule. Per Figure 2.4, glycolytic
endurance pairs well with strength-endurance-anaerobic and aerobic restoration; new-install
technical work, if it is the priority for the day, should stay the dominant, first task of
its own session (per Figure 2.3, new-skill acquisition needs a well-rested or only slightly
fatigued athlete), with strength-endurance or conditioning work added afterward, or moved to
a separate session entirely, rather than demoted to a secondary slot after glycolytic work.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 38, printed p. 27): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration: fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. Original prescribed durations: about four weeks each for accumulation and
transformation, two weeks for realization (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22); more generally,
mesocycle-blocks run about 2-6 weeks, the time needed for morphological, organic, and
biochemical adaptation (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper
(Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's 1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term
**transformation**; from section 1.2.2 onward, starting at PDF p. 38, printed p. 27 (not
p.26 as the offset alone would suggest), and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together; see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches
accumulation/transmutation/realization directly from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.65,
in the same slide block that names "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source, marker
p.64). The department's own preparatory-period design, hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic
strength, then strength-to-power (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48), is a separate general-to-specific progression, not a
restatement of A-T-R; it is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect
superimposition logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Inference (beyond
this review's scope, flagged during this fix pass since it repeats the same Bompa problem
found in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]):** the vault's Bompa & Haff
material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`) describes a
comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a 4-12 week delayed rebound, a
longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's roughly two-month training stage
(below); the two should be read as convergent, not identical, prescriptions, and a program
note should say which model's timing a given plan follows.

**Example** — **Inference:** a training stage built for a mid-season peak using the book's
own prescribed durations (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): about 4 weeks of accumulation (aerobic
base, general strength), about 4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 2 weeks of realization (tapered volume,
high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition or test
date.

[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (a different three-block taxonomy
from the same era, worth distinguishing from this one),
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]],
[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]].

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature", a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter; developed in Chapter 3, now ingested, see `_book.md`).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
not itself a benefits list. A second, five-item benefit summary appears later in the chapter
(PDF p. 44, printed p. 33), largely repeating the first four points and adding a fifth: "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks; the same
mechanism underlies [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21). This Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.
19, printed p. 8, the same claim flagged in
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) is disputed by Issurin's own later
peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block
Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text
cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**
Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may also bear on the "does not work
well" claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far (`periodization--bompa/_book.md`:
Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending), so it cannot ground this contest yet;
check once those chapters are ingested.

**Example** — **Inference:** a five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm), 14-25 day intervals, across winter ~20 days and
spring/summer 135 days (**Inference:** 155 days combined; the table gives the two figures
separately, not a single summed span). Issurin's summary point, stated on the preceding page
(PDF p. 23, printed p. 12): these athletes' 5-8 month competitive spans "can not be
subdivided into traditional preparatory and competitive periods," yet their basic abilities
(max strength, aerobic regeneration capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire
span.

**Why it works: this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
from a controlled study of periodization models.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log's "peaking phase structure" gap, this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, now ingested; see `_book.md`) is read.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
than a chosen sequence of meets; the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
was defined or verified for each performance.

**Example** — **Inference:** when explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season
programming assumes more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable,
real-world existence proof that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season; useful
for framing, not for directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

p.26 as the offset alone would suggest), and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together; see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches
accumulation/transmutation/realization directly from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.65,
in the same slide block that names "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source, marker
p.64). The department's own preparatory-period design, hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic
strength, then strength-to-power (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48), is a separate general-to-specific progression, not a
restatement of A-T-R; it is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect
superimposition logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Inference (beyond
this review's scope, flagged during this fix pass since it repeats the same Bompa problem
found in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]):** the vault's Bompa & Haff
material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`) describes a
comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a 4-12 week delayed rebound, a
longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's roughly two-month training stage
(below); the two should be read as convergent, not identical, prescriptions, and a program
note should say which model's timing a given plan follows.

**Example** — **Inference:** a training stage built for a mid-season peak using the book's
own prescribed durations (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): about 4 weeks of accumulation (aerobic
base, general strength), about 4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 2 weeks of realization (tapered volume,
high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition or test
date.

**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (a different three-block taxonomy
from the same era, worth distinguishing from this one),
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]],
[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]].

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature", a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter; developed in Chapter 3, now ingested, see `_book.md`).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
not itself a benefits list. A second, five-item benefit summary appears later in the chapter
(PDF p. 44, printed p. 33), largely repeating the first four points and adding a fifth: "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks; the same
mechanism underlies [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21). This Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.
19, printed p. 8, the same claim flagged in
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) is disputed by Issurin's own later
peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block
Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text
cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**
Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may also bear on the "does not work
well" claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far (`periodization--bompa/_book.md`:
Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending), so it cannot ground this contest yet;
check once those chapters are ingested.

**Example** — **Inference:** a five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm), 14-25 day intervals, across winter ~20 days and
spring/summer 135 days (**Inference:** 155 days combined; the table gives the two figures
separately, not a single summed span). Issurin's summary point, stated on the preceding page
(PDF p. 23, printed p. 12): these athletes' 5-8 month competitive spans "can not be
subdivided into traditional preparatory and competitive periods," yet their basic abilities
(max strength, aerobic regeneration capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire
span.

**Why it works: this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
from a controlled study of periodization models.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log's "peaking phase structure" gap, this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, now ingested; see `_book.md`) is read.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
than a chosen sequence of meets; the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
was defined or verified for each performance.

**Example** — **Inference:** when explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season
programming assumes more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable,
real-world existence proof that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season; useful
for framing, not for directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

**Why it works: the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** — Issurin
does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative
three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer
throwers training under one coach; one Olympic final's podium (plus unspecified "other
Olympic Games" results). This is a single coach's outcome with no comparison group, no
report of what other finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and
Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy;
see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
historically related, three-block system.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should
specify which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type
blocks) and should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one
documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]], a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault): the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay

**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
concentrated blocks.

**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
improve; explosive strength *decreased*, despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation has two separate
parts: extensive endurance work captures the metabolic energy needed for post-exercise
anabolism, which suppresses muscle hypertrophy; separately, coaches' and athletes'
observations show that a strenuous, high-volume training program causes permanent fatigue,
keeping central and peripheral neural factors far from the optimum needed for improving
muscular contraction. Klausen (1990) is cited for a more general point about what conditions
the neural mechanism (state of the CNS, sensitivity of the neuro-motor pool), not for the
fatigue observation specifically.

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic

needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system

Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative

(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer
throwers training under one coach; one Olympic final's podium (plus unspecified "other
Olympic Games" results). This is a single coach's outcome with no comparison group, no
report of what other finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and
Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics

talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and

blocks) and should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one
documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]], a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault): the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design

**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume," and "the prevailing opinion was that
this load level was excessive and that the training design could be made more effective."
The block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and proved in
practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of
the mesocycles was set "according to physiological and biochemical prerequisites that
usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable
improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive
outcomes: three gold and three silver medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold
medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990) at the World Championships.

**Why it works: the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
equipment, competitor turnover).

**When to apply: untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
design at scale (not just with one athlete).

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The book gives the source publication as Issurin &
Kaverin (1985) but does not itself state what Issurin's own role on the national team was.
**Inference:** reading this as the concept's inventor reporting on his own uncontrolled
intervention with his own national team is a reasonable inference from the shared authorship
and the book's framing, not something the text says outright. Either way, the account here
(2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
training volume."

**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
evidence.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session

**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
scrimmage or sparring session plays the role), the single most important exercise, given
priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 66, printed p. 55, based on Fox &

**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).

quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43), Issurin's own adaptation of
Borg's scale to workout load levels, not a direct reproduction of Borg 1973, offers a
parallel mapping using Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.

exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in

payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF

restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.

settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones

abandoned when athletes learned to game them). Session-RPE load tracking has its own gaming

specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time

# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design

**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume," and "the prevailing opinion was that
this load level was excessive and that the training design could be made more effective."
The block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and proved in
practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of
the mesocycles was set "according to physiological and biochemical prerequisites that
usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable
improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive
outcomes: three gold and three silver medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold
medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990) at the World Championships.

Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale

same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
equipment, competitor turnover).

as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
design at scale (not just with one athlete).

Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;

evidence.

# A Morning Full-Body Resistance Workout Did Not Hurt Jump, Anaerobic Power, or Shooting Accuracy Six Hours Later

**What it is** — Woolstenhulme et al. (2004), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 80, printed p. 69):
highly trained female basketball players (ages 18-22; exact sample size not stated in this
text) completed a within-subject comparison on two separate days. On the experimental day,
they performed a full-body morning resistance workout (7 exercises, 3-6 sets, 5-12RM loads),
then after **six hours of rest** were tested on vertical jump, a 30-second Wingate anaerobic
cycling test, and a 60-second shooting-accuracy trial. On the control day, the same test
battery was completed without the preceding resistance workout. Statistical analysis found
no differences between the athletes' results on the experimental vs. control days. Issurin's
stated conclusion: "a high-resistance full-body workout of moderate intensity has no negative
impact on the manifestation of sport-specific athletic abilities of trained basketball
players after six hours of rest."

**Why it works: inference, not stated in the cited passage** — Six hours appears to be
sufficient for the acute neuromuscular fatigue from a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume
resistance session (5-12RM, 7 exercises) to resolve enough that it does not measurably
degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a skill-accuracy task; Issurin does not present the
physiological recovery mechanism in this passage beyond citing the outcome.

**When to apply** — Issurin frames this as an additional comment on sequencing resistance
workouts and game practice "in dual and team sports," where "regular strength training is an
indispensable part of in-season preparation on professional and semi-professional teams"
(PDF p. 79, printed p. 68); he does not name football specifically. **Inference:** this
applies to football, a team sport with a long competitive season, for the same practical
question: whether morning hours can be used for resistance training on a day with afternoon
practice or competition, given that in-season strength training is described elsewhere in this chapter as necessary
to offset the "dramatic losses of lean body mass, and maximum and explosive strength" a long
20-35 week competitive season can otherwise cause (Baker, 2001; Gamble, 2006, as cited by
Issurin, PDF pp. 79-80). This gives a specific, citable data point (six hours, moderate
5-12RM loading) supporting a same-day AM-lift/PM-practice-or-game model, consistent with
Eric's baseline's general in-season rule to "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than
avoid lifting in-season (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21).

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The cited sample is female basketball players; exact
sample size, loading specifics beyond "5-12RM," and effect-size/statistical detail are not
given in this text, so the finding should be treated as a directional result, not a precise
dosing guarantee. **Inference:** football involves substantially higher-impact,
higher-volume, and often heavier absolute loading than a 5-12RM "moderate intensity"
basketball-focused protocol, and involves collision-based rather than jump/shoot-accuracy
outcome measures; do not assume this six-hour window transfers unchanged to a heavier
football-specific lift or to contact-sport performance measures without independent
verification. The study also does not address multi-day accumulated fatigue from repeated
same-day lift-then-compete scheduling across a full season, only a single isolated
comparison day.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football program considering morning lifts on game day or heavy-practice
days has a citable data point that a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume full-body session
six hours before performance testing did not degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a
skill-accuracy measure in one studied population, but should treat football-specific
validation (heavier loads, contact-sport outcome measures) as a separate, unanswered
question.

**Related** — [[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]].

# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power

**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
