Ultimately, the BP program yielded signiﬁcantly more
favorable results than control group training impact on both
bone status and wellness estimates.
It can be suggested that the outcomes of this study
illustrate successful application of the BP approach to
specialized training programs for recreational athletes.
4 Conclusion
It would be a regrettable mistake to think that the tradi-
tional theory of training should stay the same within the
older paradigms despite the tremendous changes that have
occurred in the world of sport and the dramatic progress of
sport science. The shortcomings of traditional theory have
been noted repeatedly in previous publications [56–59],
and, in comparison, the newer innovative training concepts
look reasonable and desirable. The aim of increasing
training stimulation within the framework of traditional
theory led to a dramatic elevation in workload magnitude
and the dissemination of harmful pharmacological tech-
nologies [60]. Implementation of highly concentrated
workloads instead of further increasing training magnitude
appears to be a practical, scientiﬁcally based way to
improve the preparation of high-performance athletes.
Therefore, such coaching concepts as ‘block’, ‘block
structure’, and ‘block periodization’ have become a reality
in contemporary sport and an indispensable part of theory
of training.
The present review characterizes and differentiates
between two innovative versions of BP training approa-
ches. It was noted and should be emphasized that the CU
training model has been proven effective mostly in the
jumping disciplines, which require a relatively narrow
range of targeted abilities [4, 5]. It can be accepted that this
BP training version has the potential to improve one main
ﬁtness component, but has serious restrictions when
applied to sports and disciplines where peak performance
demands many targeted abilities. The multi-targeted BP
training model was created and implemented based on the
experiences of high-performance athletes in canoe–kayak
paddling [3, 27], track and ﬁeld [6], and swimming [7, 8].
In all these cases, sport-speciﬁc preparedness and peak
performance are ﬁrmly based on a number of targeted
abilities. The sequencing of block mesocycles focusing on
the
appropriate
combination
of
compatible
training
modalities prompts correct interaction and the superposi-
tion of training effects producing by the entire preparation
program.
The outcomes of numerous studies conducted during
recent decades give relevant information concerning the
beneﬁts and limitations of both BP training models. The
studies evaluating the effects of CU training programs
during athlete preparation in multi-targeted sports did not
indicate any remarkable positive impact on event-speciﬁc
performances [13–17]. In contrast, the beneﬁts of multi-
targeted BP training programs were supported by the
ﬁndings of 28 studies conducted in different sports. For
instance, the superiority of the multi-targeted BP training
system was conﬁrmed by the outcomes of long-term
studies with the national canoe–kayak teams of four
countries: USSR [27], Spain [28], Romania [33], and
Belorussia [36].
Apparently, both BP training versions were proposed for
the preparation of high-performance athletes. Indeed,
almost all of the studies mentioned in this paper were
conducted with elite, sub-elite, and well-trained athletes. It
was claimed that low- and medium-level athletes are suf-
ﬁciently sensitive to any kind of training stimuli and thus
can beneﬁt sufﬁciently from traditionally designed pro-
grams [60]. In fact, proper analysis gives no evidence that
amateur athletes have any
serious restrictions when
implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in
blocks of optimal duration. Moreover, the ﬁndings of the
study with aged recreational female trainees showed the
block-structured program to be considerably superior to the
traditional version [55]. These recent data make it possible

## Key findings

- The authors' professional-rugby example accumulated average weekly loads of 2,400–2,600 AU in early preseason and approximately 1,800–1,900 AU in season, including match load. [p. 4]
- In the within-week examples, two schedules with the same absolute weekly load of 2,125 AU produced different strain; the more homogeneous schedule increased strain by approximately 30%. [p. 5]
- In planned download weeks, athletes typically accumulated 70–80% of the training load from other weeks in the same block, according to the authors' applied observations. [p. 6]
- The authors recommend recording nontraining days as zero load because omitting zeros artificially inflates calculated monotony and strain. [p. 8]

## Limitations and applicability

- The article is instructional and largely experience-based; the displayed rugby examples do not report sample size, uncertainty, hypothesis tests, or injury/performance outcomes.
- Session RPE is subjective, and stable "high raters" make absolute values unsuitable for direct player-to-player comparison; the authors favor comparing each player's trend with the squad trend. [p. 8]
- Results and thresholds from two professional rugby settings should not be treated as universal targets for other teams, competitive levels, sports, or individuals.
- Timing conventions, warm-up inclusion, actual versus scheduled match duration, rest-day zeros, and fit-to-play roster definitions must remain consistent to preserve longitudinal meaning. [pp. 7-8]
- The authors conclude that session RPE should complement, rather than replace, external-load and objective internal-load monitoring. [p. 8]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use session RPE as a low-cost longitudinal layer that integrates the athlete's perceived internal load across training modalities. Define collection and duration rules before the season, audit missing rest-day zeros, and interpret individual trends rather than borrowing the article's absolute AU values as prescriptions. In Baylor American-football work, this rugby-union example may inform workflow design but requires sport-, position-, and schedule-specific calibration.

## Evidence map
======
## Key findings

- Differential-RPE models explained 66% to 91% of variance in global session-RPE load across training modes. [Table 2, p. 5]
- The strongest dimension varied by mode: leg exertion for high-intensity intervals (r = 0.67, 90% CL ±0.22), breathlessness for repeated high-intensity efforts (r = 0.89, ±0.08), cognitive/technical demand for speed (r = 0.63, ±0.17), and upper-body exertion for upper-body resistance training (r = 0.92, ±0.07). [Table 2, p. 5]
- The authors concluded that training modes elicited distinct perceptual profiles that a single score may not fully represent. [pp. 4–5]

## Limitations and applicability

- External load was not quantified as part of this study, limiting inference about why perceptual dimensions differed. [p. 4]
- Ratings were collected 15–30 minutes post-session, and the authors acknowledged a possible latency effect. [p. 2]
- The paper labels specific training substitutions as speculative and calls for further research. [p. 6]
- Practitioner transfer limitation: Associations with global RPE do not validate differential RPE as an injury predictor or prescribe universal response thresholds.

## Practitioner interpretation

Differential RPE can be added when the program needs to distinguish central, lower-limb, upper-body, or cognitive stress. Use athlete-specific trends to clarify the source of a high global load, while retaining the session plan and external-load context.

## Evidence map

18:**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.
22:**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accumulation and mismanagement tips into overtraining. The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week. Builds on [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--step-loading-paradigm]]; bounded by [[principle--individualization]].
24:**Example** — A 3-week strength-concentrated block (strength up, speed maintained) is timed so the performance rebound surfaces ~4–6 weeks later at the first key competition; T:C ratio is monitored to confirm the post-block recovery.

--- IDX 65 ---
54
 
 
 
Figure 2.2 Heart Rate workout pattern of Gal Friedman, gold medal winner in the 
windsurfing regatta at the Athens Olympic Games.  
Key-exercise, 6×1.5min pumping with 1.5min rest (by courtesy of Omrit 
Yanilov-Eden, 2005). 
 
 
Case study. Gal Friedman, a world-leading windsurfer, substantially reformed the 
traditional training approach which was based mostly on extensive long-duration 
workouts at sea. He initiated highly intense interval workouts, in which high 
efforts were produced through forceful pumping movements.  In this, the athlete 
produced propulsion by frequent flaps of the sail.  The typical key-exercise 
performed by Gal was as follows: 6 repetitions of speed movements for 1.5 
minutes with 1.5 min intervals of low intensity movement (Figure 2.2). The speed 
regime of each performance was controlled, and an HR monitor was used to 
evaluate the athlete’s response. The graph displays repetitive HR peaks at the 178 
level with subsequent reduction to 110 b/min, while his personal HR maximum 
was 198. Thus, the planned key-exercise was executed at 90% of his personal HR 
upper limit.  This load level was definitely the highest in the entire workout 
(Yanilov-Eden, 2005)  
 
 
 

--- IDX 66 ---
55
 
 
Selection of the key-exercise is of primary importance in structuring a 
workout and offers a professional challenge for coaches. Despite the illusory 
simplicity of this operation, many mistakes have been made in routine work, even by 
experienced coaches. 
 
Example. At a national coaching seminar attended by representatives who had 
earned many Olympic, World and Continental medals, participants were asked to 
put together a typical workout to develop certain motor abilities. Of the great 
variety of answers received, more than 50% were incorrect. Even experienced 
coaches confused exercises for maximal speed and speed endurance (anaerobic 
glycolitic capacity), exercises for aerobic endurance and aerobic power, etc. 
Apparently, it was time to refresh this basic knowledge.   
 
 
Describing typical key-exercises for use in any sport is an unrealistic task. 
Nevertheless, it is possible to characterize the most typical training regimes of key-
exercises to develop major motor abilities (Table 2.10).

# Round-2 review: Issurin, *Block Periodization*, Chapters 1-2 (fix verification)

Reviewer: Claude Opus 5.5, 2026-09-27. Read-only pass over the 16 Ch1-2 entries and the Ch1-2 parts of `_book.md` after the fixes logged in `staging/fixes_issurin_ch1-2_applied.md`. Ch3 files (`_scope_issurin_ch3.txt`) were not reviewed.

Method: I read every in-scope file in full and extracted the PDF text for idx 12-86 (PyMuPDF). I rendered Figure 2.3 (idx 71) as an image and checked its bar ends. Every quote or locator the fixer added or changed was checked against the page. I opened the vault briefs for every new citation (Issurin 2016, Comyns 2013, McLaren 2017, Hanson 2007, Hirayama 2014, Seitz 2017), the Bompa and Verkhoshansky entries they link to, and `week1-lecture.md`. Issurin 2016 was also read in the original (Zotero `PT9QTQ2I`, PDF pp. 6, 7, 11). Locators below use the book's convention: 0-based idx = printed + 11.

All cited vault and staging files exist: the three PAP papers, Comyns, McLaren, Issurin 2016, Bompa `principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching` / `framework--step-loading-paradigm` / `heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio`, the Moyer Bondarchuk file, and the four Verkhoshansky staging entries. The problems are in what three of them are cited *for* (rows below).

## Read this first: round 1 was wrong about Issurin 2016 (do not re-apply its correction)

Round 1 told the fixer to re-ground `contested` in the principle and training-stage entries on the vault brief for Issurin (2016). The brief says concentrated-unidirectional evidence was "insufficient" for combat, team-sport and swimming preparation [its p.6] and "restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities" [its p.11]. The fixer applied this exactly. **The correction was itself wrong.** The original paper shows:

- The "concentrated unidirectional (CU)" model is **Verkhoshansky's**, not Issurin's. Table 1 is "based on Verkhoshansky [9, 10]". The p.6 findings (basketball, handball and soccer fitness gains with no game data; swimmers 2 of 3) all come from Table 2, "Effects of concentrated unidirectional bloc periodization training programs".
- Issurin's own A-T-R model is the **multi-targeted BP** version. Section 3 starts at p.7, and p.11 names the canoe-kayak, track and swimming lineage. The review reports it is "supported by the findings of 28 studies" [p.11].
- The review does not soften the 2008 critique of the traditional model; it repeats it. CU "has no advantage over traditional planning, because it does not allow the multi-peak annual design" [p.6]. The conclusion also reads: "It would be a regrettable mistake to think that the traditional theory of training should stay the same" [p.11].

So the 2016 review cannot "dispute" the 2008 line "does not work well for high-performance athletes". Both entries now misstate a library source.

**There is a real Issurin-vs-Issurin contradiction to use instead.** It sits on the principle entry's own When NOT carve-out:

- 2008 (PDF 44 / p.33): the traditional approach "has visible benefits for the preparation of low- and mid-level athletes ... medium-level concentration still provides sufficient stimulation".
- 2016 [p.11]: "proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration". It also cites a recreational-trainee study where the block program was "considerably superior".

**Upstream note (the fixer cannot act on it; flag to Eric):** the vault brief `research-papers/issurin-2016-...md` never says that "concentrated-unidirectional" means Verkhoshansky's model, which is why this misreading happened. Its Key findings should be annotated: "CU = Verkhoshansky's model; the multi-targeted (A-T-R) model is the one the review favours."

## Entry table

| File | Round-1 verdict | Status now | Evidence (with page) | Exact remaining correction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `principle--concentration-of-training-workloads.md` | FIX | **NEW PROBLEM** [major] | (1) The Contested paragraph says the 2008 "does not work well for high-performance athletes" claim (PDF 19 / p.8, verified) "is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review", which "judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient". That finding is about Verkhoshansky's CU model (Issurin 2016 pp.6-7, Table 1 "based on Verkhoshansky"). The same review supports multi-targeted BP with 28 studies and restates the critique of the traditional model (p.6, p.11); see the section above. (2) The Eric's-baseline sentence is garbled: "...not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle", incompatible qualities are not both trained...". Checked and fixed: link to `[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]` works; Table 1.4 "There is sufficient energy supply" locator note matches idx 20; Fig 1.7 quotes (idx 37); low/mid carve-out (idx 44); Bompa 1984 (idx 13); Bompa inference relabelled; week1-lecture.md lines 1795 and 1838 confirm the Issurin attribution and "Can't ride 2 horses". | Replace the whole Contested paragraph with: "**Contested (Issurin 2008 vs Issurin 2016):** this book limits the concentration principle to high-level athletes, saying medium-level concentration 'still provides sufficient stimulation' for low- and mid-level athletes (PDF 44 / p.33). Issurin's later review says 'proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration' (Issurin 2016, p.11, `research-papers/issurin-2016-...`). The same review restricts only Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, where many interacting abilities are needed (pp.6-7). It supports Issurin's own multi-targeted block model (28 studies, p.11) and repeats the 2008 critique of traditional planning, so it does not dispute 'does not work well for high-performance athletes' (PDF 19 / p.8). Its 28-study support is an author-curated, non-systematic synthesis." Keep `contested`, with this as the stated reason. Rewrite the baseline sentence: "Eric's baseline: the course teaches this rule from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67), filed as 'you can't ride two horses with one saddle': incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, ... class1 transcript pp.28-29)." Optional: drop "independently" from the Bompa convergence sentence, because the T:C concentrated-loading model is Verkhoshansky-lineage and independence is not shown. |

The Contested paragraph cites Issurin 2016 p.6 (team and combat CU studies with no game data) as "a direct qualification of the confident five-benefit list above". ## Read this first: round 1 was wrong about Issurin 2016 (do not re-apply its correction)

Round 1 told the fixer to re-ground `contested` in the principle and training-stage entries on the vault brief for Issurin (2016). The brief says concentrated-unidirectional evidence was "insufficient" for combat, team-sport and swimming preparation [its p.6] and "restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities" [its p.11]. The fixer applied this exactly. **The correction was itself wrong.** The original paper shows:

- The "concentrated unidirectional (CU)" model is **Verkhoshansky's**, not Issurin's. Table 1 is "based on Verkhoshansky [9, 10]". The p.6 findings (basketball, handball and soccer fitness gains with no game data; swimmers 2 of 3) all come from Table 2, "Effects of concentrated unidirectional bloc periodization training programs".
- Issurin's own A-T-R model is the **multi-targeted BP** version. Section 3 starts at p.7, and p.11 names the canoe-kayak, track and swimming lineage. The review reports it is "supported by the findings of 28 studies" [p.11].
- The review does not soften the 2008 critique of the traditional model; it repeats it. CU "has no advantage over traditional planning, because it does not allow the multi-peak annual design" [p.6]. The conclusion also reads: "It would be a regrettable mistake to think that the traditional theory of training should stay the same" [p.11].

So the 2016 review cannot "dispute" the 2008 line "does not work well for high-performance athletes". Both entries now misstate a library source.

**There is a real Issurin-vs-Issurin contradiction to use instead.** It sits on the principle entry's own When NOT carve-out:

- 2008 (PDF 44 / p.33): the traditional approach "has visible benefits for the preparation of low- and mid-level athletes ... medium-level concentration still provides sufficient stimulation".
- 2016 [p.11]: "proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration". It also cites a recreational-trainee study where the block program was "considerably superior".

**Upstream note (the fixer cannot act on it; flag to Eric):** the vault brief `research-papers/issurin-2016-...md` never says that "concentrated-unidirectional" means Verkhoshansky's model, which is why this misreading happened.
